html:
From 1640 to 1796 the Dutch East India Company held the coasts of Sri Lanka, then called Ceylon, and ran the island's cinnamon trade as a tight monopoly.

The Dutch took Galle in 1640, Colombo in 1656 and Jaffna in 1658, and then kept the coasts for themselves. The kingdom of Kandy, their former ally against the Portuguese, held the hill country inside.

The prize was cinnamon, the bark of a tree that grew wild in the island's forests and was then found almost nowhere else. The Company forced men of the Salagama caste, whose traditional work was peeling cinnamon, to deliver set amounts each year. It then sold the spice in Europe at prices it fixed, and is said to have burned surplus to keep the price high.

The Dutch left forts such as Galle Fort, Dutch Roman law that still shapes Sri Lankan family law, and a Burgher community of mixed descent. The British took the coasts in 1796 and, in 1815, Kandy too, making all of Ceylon a colony.
sum: From 1640 to 1796 the Dutch East India Company held the coasts of Sri Lanka, then called Ceylon, and ran the island's cinnamon trade as a tight monopoly.
